state.question: Why does the pendulum period show elevated variance and occasional excursions beyond the baseline range (up to 1.7102 beats on day 9, down to 1.6306 on day 10) when the apparatus was stable during the initial 10-day calibration phase?

hypotheses.label: Normal measurement scatter within expected instrumental precision
hypotheses.rationale: The baseline (n=110, mean 1.6662) established over days 1–10 likely contains similar internal variance. Days 8–10 readings scatter around the baseline mean with no obvious drift direction. Standard deviation of full dataset appears ~0.025 beats; individual excursions to 1.7102 or 1.6306 are ~1.7σ and ~1.4σ respectively—not implausible for 110 trials. No systematic trend visible. This remains the null hypothesis absent evidence of genuine change.

hypotheses.label: Systematic temperature drift in the lab (day 8–10 warmer or cooler than day 1–7)
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum period is exquisitely sensitive to thermal expansion of the pivot and bob. A systematic rise in lab temperature from day 1–7 to days 8–10 would lengthen the effective pendulum length and increase period. Days 8–10 mean is 1.6675 beats vs. days 1–7 mean ~1.6655 beats—a +0.0020 beat shift, consistent with modest warming. However: (i) the shift is tiny relative to scatter; (ii) I have not yet logged lab temperature during baseline phase, so cannot confirm this; (iii) if real, temperature would need to stabilize sharply by day 10 to avoid runaway drift.

hypotheses.label: Operator or apparatus setup variation (inconsistent release height, friction, timing jitter)
hypotheses.rationale: If days 1–10 baseline was recorded under strict protocol, but days 8–10 trials introduced any slack in procedure (e.g., slightly looser release grip, wider amplitude swings, timing pick-off drift), period scatter would increase. The day 8–10 variance looks similar to baseline in magnitude, but any systematic relaxation would show as bimodal or increasing scatter. Days 8–10 readings do not cluster separately; they mingle with the baseline range. This suggests operator drift is not driving the pattern.

hypotheses.label: Instrumental creep or mechanical wear in the pendulum apparatus
hypotheses.rationale: Wear on the pivot bearing or creep in the suspension would typically show monotonic drift—increasing or decreasing period over successive trials. The data show no such monotonic trend across days 8–10. Excursions are bidirectional and uncorrelated with trial order. Wear is a real risk over weeks, but after only 10 days of use (110 trials) in a controlled lab, this is premature.

hypotheses.label: Environmental disturbance (vibration, magnetic field, air pressure) during days 8–10
hypotheses.rationale: Seismic activity, nearby machinery, or atmospheric pressure swings could perturb a sensitive pendulum. However: (i) excursions are small and scattered, not clustered by day; (ii) no report of felt tremors or equipment alarms; (iii) Meridian's settlement location and infrastructure status unknown, but absent external testimony this is speculative.
